scene.testo: Four hundred thirty miles per hour of nothing. No, wait. Seventeen thousand five hundred miles per hour. That is how fast your dinner is traveling right now. Imagine you are floating in the station at 6 AM, and breakfast is flying past your face.

Your coffee is a plastic pouch with a straw. Your eggs are dried powder. Your hands are the only table you have. Let go of anything, and it drifts away. Welcome to the strangest kitchen ever built, 250 miles above Earth.

Here is the shocking part. Astronauts eat roughly the same calories you do, but every ounce of their food was launched on a rocket. Every meal has a price tag, and every crumb is a danger. So what do they really eat?

We know this from NASA documents, from station tours filmed by the crews themselves, and from the astronauts' own accounts. Where facts are uncertain, we will tell you. First, you need to understand the one rule that shapes every meal in orbit.

Weight. Launching cargo to orbit costs thousands of dollars per pound, according to NASA estimates. So every food package is planned, weighed, and counted. Nothing is wasted. Even the water you drink may have been your own sweat a day earlier.

Now picture the pantry. Shelves of sealed pouches, cans, and packets strapped to the walls. Labels with each crew member's name. Colored tags marking breakfast, lunch, and dinner. It looks less like a restaurant and more like a supply depot.

Astronauts help plan their menus before launch. They taste dozens of items on the ground and pick favorites. NASA says the goal is variety, because bland food leads to eating less, and eating less is a real health risk in orbit.

Most food comes in three forms. Rehydrated, thermostabilized, and ready to eat. Rehydrated means dried food you rebuild with water. Thermostabilized means heat-treated and sealed in pouches or cans. Ready to eat means just open and go.

Take the dried meals. Shrimp cocktail, a famous favorite. Macaroni and cheese. Scrambled eggs. You inject hot water through a small port, squeeze the pouch, wait a few minutes, and cut it open with scissors. Dinner is served.

Hot water on the station comes from a dispenser that supplies both hot and room temperature water, according to NASA. Cold water for drinks, hot water for meals. And no, you cannot just boil a pot. There is no stove up there.

What about heating dinner? Astronauts use a food warmer, a small suitcase-sized oven that heats pouches and cans. It warms food to a safe, pleasant temperature. Nothing is cooked from scratch. Everything arrives finished, you just bring it back to life.

Then there are the tortillas. Astronauts use tortillas instead of bread, and for a very good reason. Bread makes crumbs. In weightlessness, crumbs float into eyes, noses, and equipment. A tortilla stays in one piece. Problem solved.

Peanut butter, honey, and tortillas became a station favorite. Astronauts have described making little wraps and eating them in midair. It sounds silly, but it is practical, fast, and gives you something that feels like real food.

Salt and pepper are not what you picture. Loose grains would float and clog filters or drift into eyes. So astronauts use liquid versions, salt dissolved in water and pepper suspended in oil, squeezed from small dropper bottles.

Now imagine the drinks. Orange juice powder, lemonade, coffee, tea, all in sealed pouches. You add water, shake, and sip through a straw. Pour a drink into an open cup, and in weightlessness it forms a floating blob.

Coffee got an upgrade. A special cup was designed so liquid creeps up its inside edge by surface tension, according to NASA. Astronauts could finally sip espresso from something that looks like a real cup, not a bag.

Fizzy drinks are a different story. In weightlessness, bubbles do not rise out of a liquid the way they do on Earth. Carbonated drinks have been tried in space, but the experience was reported as unpleasant. Gas stays trapped inside.

So how does anything taste up there? This is a real, documented problem. In orbit, fluids shift toward the head, and astronauts often report stuffy, congested noses. Smell dulls, and taste depends heavily on smell. Food seems blander.

That is why astronauts crave strong flavors. Hot sauce, spicy foods, and horseradish are popular, according to NASA and astronaut accounts. Shrimp cocktail is loved partly because its sauce has a real kick. Bold taste cuts through a stuffy nose.

Now step back in time. The very first American meals in space were nothing like this. They came in squeezable tubes, like toothpaste, and bite-sized cubes. Early astronauts ate pureed food straight from aluminum tubes. Not exactly appetizing.

On February 20, 1962, John Glenn orbited Earth in the Friendship 7 capsule. NASA records say he tested eating applesauce from a tube. It proved a simple point. A human being can swallow food in weightlessness. That mattered a lot.

Doctors had worried that swallowing might fail without gravity. It did not. Glenn's test showed that food moves down your throat by muscle action, not by falling. That one applesauce tube was a real milestone for human spaceflight.

By the Gemini missions in the mid-1960s, astronauts got freeze-dried food in plastic bags. Add water, wait, and eat. NASA records say many early freeze-dried items were disliked, and some crews complained about taste and texture.

Then came Apollo. For the first time, astronauts could use a spoon. Some meals came in a spoon-bowl pouch. You cut it open, and the food stuck to the spoon by surface tension. It felt closer to a real dinner.

On Apollo 8, in December 1968, the crew had hot water available for the first time on a mission to the Moon. Hot meals made a huge difference on a journey of nearly a quarter million miles away from home.

Apollo 11 astronauts ate meals on their way to the Moon in July 1969. Menus included bacon squares, peaches, coffee, and sugar cookies, according to NASA's records. Even on the most daring trip in history, breakfast mattered.

Skylab, America's first space station, launched in 1973, had something new. A real dining table where the crew could sit and eat together. They even had a food freezer and a refrigerator, a luxury no earlier crew had enjoyed.

Skylab's menu had around 70 different foods, according to NASA. Steak, ice cream, and fresh bread were reportedly among the items. Astronauts ate in shifts, strapping their feet down to stay put while eating from trays with heated compartments.

Now fast forward to the Space Shuttle era. Shuttle crews had a small galley with an oven and a water dispenser. They ate three meals a day, and every astronaut had assigned pantry lockers. It felt almost like camping, in orbit.

Shuttle astronauts could even snack. Fruit, nuts, granola bars, and candy were stashed in lockers. And a long mission meant a long wish list. Many astronauts have said that treats from home were the best morale booster in orbit.

Today's crews live on the International Space Station, which orbits at about 250 miles up. Six or seven people live there at a time. Food comes from many countries, including the United States, Russia, Japan, and Europe.

Crews often share meals together at the dining table in the Russian segment or in the US segment. Many astronauts say mealtime is the main social moment of the day. Eating together keeps a small crew feeling like a family.

Fresh food is rare and precious. When a cargo ship arrives, it sometimes carries fresh fruit and vegetables. Apples, oranges, and tomatoes get eaten fast, because they spoil quickly and the crew has been craving something crisp.

Then there is the garden. NASA's Veggie experiment grew red romaine lettuce on the station. In August 2015, crew members tasted lettuce grown in orbit for the first time. NASA reported they harvested and ate it fresh.

The crew also grew zinnia flowers and later chile peppers in orbit, according to NASA. In 2021, astronauts harvested peppers and used them in tacos. It was a small step toward growing real food far from Earth.

Why does this matter? A trip to Mars could take years, and you cannot resupply from home. NASA studies how crops might help feed future crews on long missions. It is still research, and many questions remain unanswered.

Now compare this to your kitchen. You open a fridge, pour a glass, and sit down. An astronaut straps in, adds hot water to a bag, and chases floating droplets. Same hunger, completely different rules, and every bite is carefully managed.

Cleanup matters too. Loose crumbs and droplets are wiped up with towels right away. Astronauts have said that even a tiny floating crumb can drift into a vent or someone's eye. Messes in orbit are never really somebody else's problem.

And what about trash? Food packaging gets bagged and stowed. Cargo ships carry waste away, and many burn up in the atmosphere on the way down. Every wrapper you toss in orbit has a longer journey than any wrapper on Earth.

Exercise changes appetite too. Astronauts work out about two hours a day to protect muscles and bones, according to NASA. That means they need real fuel. Eating enough is part of the mission, just like fixing equipment is.

Now the water. Station systems recover water from many sources, including moisture in the air and urine, then clean it for drinking. NASA has said its recovery system reclaims a large share of the water on board. Nothing goes to waste.

Astronauts have joked about it for years. Yesterday's coffee is today's coffee. It sounds shocking, but the water is tested and treated before anyone drinks it. When your supply line is 250 miles straight up, recycling is survival.

And here is the most surprising detail. In orbit, a dinner can include a pouch from Houston, a snack from Moscow, a treat from Tokyo, and a pepper grown on board. Six or seven people, one table, and dinner from around the world.

descrizione:
What do astronauts actually eat in space? From squeezable tubes on early missions to tortillas, rehydrated shrimp cocktail, and lettuce grown in orbit, this documentary shows what life is really like at mealtime on the International Space Station. Learn how food is stored, heated, and eaten in weightlessness, why crumbs are dangerous, and why food tastes different in orbit.

We use documented facts from NASA, ESA, and astronauts' own accounts, covering Mercury, Gemini, Apollo, Skylab, the Space Shuttle, and today's station. All footage comes from real NASA archives.
